n: Justice depends on honest testimony. Israelites must not spread false rumors or team up with wrongdoers by testifying falsely in court.

f.g: Spread or accept a false rumor.

n: Don’t go along with the crowd when the crowd is wrong, and don’t twist your testimony just to side with the majority. Truth is not decided by popular vote.

f.w: follow a multitude to do evil

n: Fairness cuts both ways: a judge must not favor a poor person simply because he is poor. Justice must be impartial.

f.g: Show favor to, take sides with.

n: Kindness extends even to enemies. If you find your enemy’s stray animal, return it. Jesus later taught, “Love your enemies.”
If your enemy’s donkey has collapsed under its load, you may feel like walking past — but you must stop and help. Shared work can soften hostility.

f.g: Help him unload and raise the animal.

n: The poor must not be denied justice in court. Verses 3 and 6 together demand true impartiality.
Stay away from false accusations, and never cause the death of an innocent person. God Himself will not declare the guilty innocent.
Bribes corrupt judgment. A gift can blind even a wise person and make a good person twist his words.
God repeats His command to protect foreigners, appealing to Israel’s own experience: you know how it feels to be an outsider.

f.w: ye know the heart of a stranger

n: The farmland was to be worked for six years in a row.
Every seventh year the land rested, and whatever grew on its own was left for the poor and for wild animals. This “sabbatical year” taught trust in God and care for the needy.
The weekly Sabbath gave rest not only to the family but to servants, foreigners, and animals. God’s rest was meant for everyone, especially those with the least control over their time.

f.w: on the seventh day thou shalt rest

n: Be careful to keep all these commands, and don’t even invoke the names of other gods — whether in oaths or prayers.

f.w: make no mention of the name of other gods

n: Israel was to gather to worship the Lord at three annual festivals.
The first is the Feast of Unleavened Bread, held with Passover in the spring, remembering the Exodus. Worshippers were to bring an offering rather than come empty-handed.

f.g: “Ear of grain” — the spring month later called Nisan (March–April).

n: The second is the Feast of Harvest (later called Weeks or Pentecost) at the grain harvest; the third is the Feast of Ingathering (Tabernacles or Booths) in the fall when all crops were gathered.

f.g: Also called the Feast of Weeks; in Greek, Pentecost.
Also called the Feast of Tabernacles or Booths.

n: At these three times every male was to come before the Lord. These pilgrimages bound the nation together in worship.

f.g: Hebrew Adonai YHWH; in the KJV, small-capital GOD represents the divine name.

n: Sacrificial blood was not to be offered with leavened (yeast) bread, and the fat of the Passover offering was not to be left overnight.
The very first of the harvest belonged to the Lord. The odd command not to boil a young goat in its mother’s milk may reject a pagan ritual or teach respect for the bond between mother and young.

f.w: Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk

n: God promises to send His Angel to guide and protect Israel all the way to the promised land. He goes before them and prepares their place.

f.g: Hebrew mal’ak — messenger. Here a divine messenger bearing God’s own authority.

f.w: the place which I have prepared

n: Israel must obey this messenger, because God’s name — His authority and presence — is in him. Many Christians see here the premortal Christ, Jehovah, who leads His people.

f.g: He carries God’s full authority and represents Him.

n: If Israel obeys, God will fight their battles; their enemies become His enemies.
The Angel will bring them into Canaan, home to many peoples whom God will remove.

f.w: Amorites, and the Hittites, and the Perizzites

n: Israel must not adopt Canaanite religion but tear down its idols and sacred pillars. The concern was spiritual: false worship would destroy Israel’s covenant.

f.g: Hebrew matsebot — standing stone pillars used in pagan worship.

n: Serving the Lord brings practical blessings: food and water blessed and sickness removed.
God promises fertility for herds and families and full, long lives for the faithful.

f.w: number of thy days I will fulfil
f.g: You will live out a full lifespan.

n: God’s reputation would go ahead of Israel, filling their enemies with dread so that they would flee.
God would send “hornets” to drive out the inhabitants — whether literal insects or a figure for panic and terror sent ahead of Israel.
The conquest would not happen all at once, so that the land would not become empty and overrun by wild animals.
God would drive them out gradually as Israel grew large enough to fill the land. Like many of God’s works, the promise unfolds step by step.
God sets Israel’s ideal borders: from the Red Sea (Gulf of Aqaba) to the Mediterranean, and from the wilderness to the Euphrates. These limits were most nearly reached under David and Solomon.
Israel must not make treaties with the Canaanites or their gods. Covenant loyalty belonged to the Lord alone.
If the Canaanites remained, their worship would trap Israel. The book of Judges later shows this exact warning coming true.
